jobs/x: Layer norm runs on every token's vector, in every layer. Here is one token's four features as bars: one, minus five, five and seven.
jobs/center: Its first job is to re-center. Subtract the mean, two, and every bar slides down, until they balance on zero.
jobs/scale: Its second job is to re-scale. Divide by the standard deviation, and the bars shrink, or stretch, to a standard spread of one.
jobs/cost: Both jobs cost arithmetic on every token, and that slows the whole network down.
jobs/bet: In 2019, Biao Zhang and Rico Sennrich bet that only the re-scaling matters. They dropped the re-centering, and divided by a root mean square instead. They called it R M S Norm: R M S, for root mean square.
jobs/result: In their tests, it did about as well as layer norm, and cut running time by between seven and sixty four percent, depending on the model.
rms/size: To re-scale, you need one number for how big the entries are. Their mean will not do: the signs cancel, and one, minus five, five and seven average just two.
rms/socket: Electricians met this long ago. An American wall socket swings between about plus and minus a hundred and seventy volts, so its average is zero. The hundred and twenty volts it is rated at is a root mean square.
rms/sq: The name is the recipe, read backwards. Square every entry: one, twenty five, twenty five, forty nine. A square is never negative, so nothing cancels.
rms/mean: Take the mean of the squares: a hundred over four, twenty five.
rms/root: Then the root: five. It undoes the squaring, so the answer is back in the entries' own units. That is the root mean square of x, written R M S of x: the size of a typical entry.
rms/out: Divide by it: zero point two, minus one, one, and one point four. Now the root mean square is exactly one.
rms/gain: Last, each feature is multiplied by its own learned gain, gamma, which starts at one.
rms/params: There is no shift, beta, so with d features, R M S Norm learns d numbers, where layer norm learns two d.
shift/scale: Triple the vector, and its root mean square triples as well: fifteen. Divide, and the output is exactly the same as before.
shift/shift: But shift every entry up by three. R M S Norm never subtracts the mean, so its output moves.
shift/ln: Layer norm would subtract the new mean, and the shift would vanish. That is the whole price of dropping the mean: blind to scale, but not to a shift.
